Hi friends. I've read a lot of misinformation and figured I'd use my degree to help you become more informed.

Weed is technically physically addictive (read: habit forming) as scientists have found it has an affect on your body's dopamine systems through GABA. All abused drugs increase the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Cannabinoids do so indirectly. They inhibit GABA release in the ventral segmental area of the midbrain, a major source of axons that release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. When they inhibit GABA there they decrease inhibition (increasing activity) of the neurons that release dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. The dopamine spike is the reason for the addictiveness of most commonly abused drugs.

So in short marijuana is physically habit forming, like most drugs, though it's not as serious about it as some drugs- as cited by a user on this post cannabis leaves your fat cells slowly and over time, mitigating withdrawal symptoms. I've heard many users claim it's only psychologically addictive, but I'm fairly sure any experienced pot smoker will tell you how he or she becomes anxious stopping after a week or so of constant smoking.

I think what's important is the degree to which this has a practical effect. I'm sure coffee does something very similar, and I know from personal experience that abrupt withdrawal from a regular coffee habit is certainly something you will feel, but I think most of us would hesitate to use the word 'addictive' to describe it.

In fact, I think that word is so overloaded and so often misapplied that I prefer not to use it at all. We can more accurately describe these effects by using other terms that are more precise.

On a physical level, weed, like coffee, normally produces mild physical and emotional discomfort when withdrawn after moderate levels of use. Heavy users can expect to experience more of an effect, and should probably taper down first. Light users might not notice anything. The effects are short-term and can be expected to be gone within a week. Psychological dependance can be a much bigger issue, but again, it's on the same order of magnitude that we see with people who are psychologically dependent on things like overeating. Indeed, I think there is an excellent scientific case to me made that overeating is a more intractable psychological dependance than weed is. What percentage of chronic overeaters ever manage to loose weight and keep it off for two years? Last I saw it was well below five percent. I doubt very much that 95% of heavy weed smokers continue until they die, even if they struggle against it. It's just not that hard to quit.

If you want to discuss overeating, I've read studies that cite certain types of commonly used sugars as up to 6 times more addictive than cocaine. There's a reason 1/3 of Americans are obese, and it's because sugar-loaded food is extraordinarily addictive to the point that cocaine-addicted rats prefer sugar water, once exposed for a set amount of time, to cocaine.

This seems so silly.

Humans aren't entirely rational; we are deeply emotional beings. The subconscious and unconscious are powerful, and easily override the rational conscious part of our minds when it comes to making decisions. We are attracted to friends that get us into trouble, we fall in love with people we know will hurt us, we drink knowing we'll get a hangover, we buy things we don't need on credit. Marketers have been taking advantage of this from the early days of psychoanalysis in the 1920s and 1930s: advertizing went from describing a product and its usefulness (appealing to the rational) to trying to build associations with the product and desirable emotional states (usually via something to do with sex). And where marketers blazed a trail, politicians have followed: so much campaigning today is on an emotional level, rather than coldly weighing the facts related to policy.

Libertarianism ignores the entirety of human history, which is mainly just one story after another of power bases being formed, consolidated, and used to enrich their leaders.
